Some were started by residents or local groups, some are announced by a community council on a paper notice, and some come from the district’s children’s centers; a badge on each shows who is behind it. These are not city announcements, so please check the details with each source.

comm_act_intro: Community Councils carry out a wide range of activities that span generations.
comm_act_list:
• Disaster preparedness & safety: Organizing and participating in area-wide disaster drills, preparing evacuation-shelter manuals, disaster imagination games (DIG)
  • Crime prevention: Forming blue-light patrol teams, creating safety maps, watching over children
  • Children's events: Kite-flying, mochi-pounding, walk rallies, sports meets, and more
  • Community exchange: Summer festivals, fireworks shows, music festivals
  • Senior support: Wellness salons, Orange Cafés (dementia cafés), neighborhood helper teams
  • Digital support: Smartphone classes
comm_act_note: The city groups local issues into four areas — disaster preparedness, crime prevention, welfare, and exchange — and each council plans its projects along these lines.
comm_base_p: As the name "○○ Elementary School District" implies, the elementary school district is the geographic foundation of each Community Council. School districts serve as units of social cohesion, and Community Councils use this framework to cultivate horizontal connections among residents.
comm_card_list: 📋 The five Community Councils of the Shinooka area
comm_club_p: After-school childcare clubs for children of dual-income families are also organized on a school-district basis and operate in coordination with Community Councils and PTAs. After the reorganization, a club is to be set up inside each of Tokadai Higashi and Tokadai Nishi elementary schools (FAQ).
comm_consider1:
Schools and community ties
Schools bring together not only children but also parents and local residents. Events such as sports days, school presentations and evacuation drills are also occasions for people of different generations to meet. For this reason, school mergers are often described as affecting not only the learning environment but also how local people are connected.
comm_consider2:
Points raised when organizations cover a wider area
A wider area can make it easier to pool people and funds, and lets residents across a larger area work together. On the other hand, taking part can become harder once activities go beyond the circle of people who know each other, and attachment to the former school district may fade. Which side comes out stronger is generally said to depend on how the transition is handled and how residents take part.
comm_consider3:
How the transition proceeds
When local organizations merge, the timing, how activities are handed over, and how residents are informed and consulted become the main issues. In the Shinooka district, the five councils are to be reorganized into two, targeting fiscal 2029, and how the merger proceeds will be decided through future discussions. At the 2025 briefings and public comment process, residents also voiced concern about the future of the local community.

comm_cs_p1: Each school in Komaki City has a School Management Council (Community School). This is a forum where parents and local residents can share opinions on the school's educational policies and operations — an important institution connecting Community Councils with schools.
comm_cs_p2: It creates opportunities for local adults to participate in classroom support, read-alouds, and career education, and to share school challenges with the wider community.
comm_def_p1: A Community Council is an organization voluntarily formed by local residents based on the elementary school district. Groups such as neighborhood associations, PTAs, senior clubs, sports clubs, and welfare commissioners participate across organizational lines to discuss local issues and revitalize community life.
comm_def_p2: In Komaki City, Community Councils have been established in 14 of the city's 16 elementary school districts (as of April 2026). The five elementary school districts in the Shinooka area (Shinooka, Hikarigaoka, Oshiro, Momogaoka, and Sue) each have their own council.

comm_events_lead: Event listings for community councils, published by Komaki City (🔄 fetched automatically every day). They cover all 16 elementary school districts in the city, so events from the five Shinooka-area councils are marked and shown first.
comm_fac_p: The gymnasiums, sports fields, and pools of each school are used daily by local residents for community sports and as disaster bases (evacuation sites). Community members also participate in school events such as sports meets and learning fairs, making schools serve as the public "face" of the community.
comm_kz_c1_h: What is the mid-term review of the Eastern District Development Strategy?
comm_kz_c1_p: The strategy is a ten-year policy drawn up in March 2022, and this fiscal year is its midpoint. The draft looks back at the work so far and revises part of the policies and the reference indicators. Its outcome indicator is the working-age share (ages 15–64) of the eastern district's population: by census figures it was 58.4% in 2020, with targets of 54.0% for FY2026 and 50.7% for FY2031. Because the 2025 census results are not yet out, the draft shows, for reference, the share counted from the resident register (59.3% in 2020, 55.7% in 2025, FY2026 target 53.8%).
comm_kz_c2_h: Vacant prefectural housing units as places for exchange and community activity
comm_kz_c2_p: According to the draft, prefectural housing in the eastern district has lower occupancy than in other parts of the city, and many units have long stood vacant. In one complex (古雅) half of the units are empty, and occupancy is about 30% lower than in private apartment buildings. As one way of making use of vacant houses and vacant apartments, the draft says the city will work with Aichi Prefecture so that vacant prefectural housing units can be used as bases for multi-generation exchange and community activities.
comm_kz_c3_h: School reorganization and the land and buildings it frees up
comm_kz_c3_p: The draft says that, in addition to the former depot site of the Tokadai Line, the sites of schools after reorganization and of the heated swimming pool are expected to fall out of use, and that their use needs to be considered in a planned way based on local needs. Its measures include considering former school sites as bases for exchange and activities, and multi-generation, multicultural exchange using former school sites. It also lists as a challenge that schools and the community engage with each other across generations, taking school reorganization as the occasion.
comm_kz_c4_h: A draft to widen the kinds of shops allowed in Tokadai's detached-house areas
comm_kz_c4_p: In Tokadai's detached-house areas (Areas A and B of the district plan), the shop part (up to 50 m²) of a combined home-and-shop building may at present be used only as an office, a classroom such as a cram school, or an atelier or workshop. The city's draft would widen this to the range permitted in a Category 1 low-rise exclusive residential zone. Area C, where convenience stores and the like can be built, is not covered this time.
comm_kz_c4_p2: From April to June 2025 the city surveyed about 4,500 households living in Tokadai's detached houses. It reports that a certain number wanted eating places, food shops and places for the community to gather, and that younger respondents wanted them more. In November 2025 it heard from the heads of the 19 neighborhood units (区) that have detached houses: some said the change is “needed for future vitality,” while others said “the quiet living environment should be protected” and “those opening shops should be asked to take full care of their surroundings.” The city plans to set separate operating rules asking those who open shops to secure parking, consider their surroundings and explain their plans to residents.
comm_kz_h2: Review of the Eastern District Strategy and Land Use in Tokadai<small>東部振興構想の見直しと桃花台の土地利用</small>
comm_kz_lead: A draft mid-term review of the city's Eastern District Development Strategy (FY2022–2031), and a draft change to the district plan that would widen the kinds of shops allowed in Tokadai's detached-house areas, were presented in the materials of the city's Eastern District Development Council on November 12, 2026. Both are still drafts.
comm_kz_more: How this site sees the drafts is written in “What the draft mid-term review changes, and what it does not” on the in-depth review page.

comm_kz_pc_p: Per the city's announcement, public comments on the draft mid-term review of the Eastern District Development Strategy are being accepted from Friday, November 27 to Monday, December 28, 2026. According to the council materials, comments can be sent by mail, fax or email, or handed in at the Eastern District Development Office (東部まちづくり推進室) on the 2nd floor of the City Hall East Building. Comments that only say “for” or “against” without a reason, or that lack an address and name, are not treated as comments.

comm_leg_bonote_p: A tradition of offering old martial-art forms with staffs and other tools at shrine festivals. Okusa Bo-no-te (Shinkage school) is offered at the festival of Okusa Hachiman Shrine and Noguchi Bo-no-te (Genji Ten school) at that of Noguchi Shinmei Shrine, both every year on the second Sunday of October. Both are intangible folk cultural properties designated by the city. They died out for a time after the war, but local people formed preservation societies, revived them and still pass them on.
comm_leg_budou_p: Grapes are widely grown alongside peaches in Kamisue, Takane, Okusa and nearby. Fifth graders at Hikarigaoka Elementary School pick grapes with the help of local grape farmers. The local “Eastern District Specialty PR Team” and grape farmers have held a parent-and-child Christmas wreath workshop using Komaki grapes, and at a local-produce cooking session people made grape juice from grape skins.
comm_leg_chigo_p: A wooded hillside on 8 hectares of prefectural forest in Oyama, cared for by a residents’ group since July 2007. The group protects wild azaleas, the city flower (about 1,200 plants counted as of March 2014), and runs nature experiences, forest play and nature watching. In spring it holds viewing walks for the Mitsuba azaleas in bloom.
comm_leg_cochin_p: The city presents Nagoya Cochin chicken as a specialty of the eastern district. According to the Shinooka Karuta, it was bred by a former Owari domain samurai who moved to Ikenouchi, started keeping chickens and crossed breeds again and again. In connection with “Nagoya Cochin Day” on 10 March, a local group holds sessions in Toryo Junior High School’s cooking room to make hikizuri-nabe, a local dish. At a market in the east, food-truck dishes using Nagoya Cochin quickly sold out.
comm_leg_farm_h: Bid for the Chunichi Dragons farm team
comm_leg_farm_p: Since May 2026 the Chunichi Dragons have been inviting bids for a new farm team base (70,000–80,000 m² of usable land, move completed in the early 2030s). Komaki has bid with a plan centered on the Sports Complex (about 92,000 m²) that also uses the site of Sue Elementary left by the reorganization, and passed the first round. Second-round proposals were due October 30, and the preferred negotiating partner is to be chosen around May 2027. The city says it is examining the effect on current sports use, traffic congestion and its own costs.
comm_leg_fest_p: At the Ikenouchi festival a preservation society keeps up festival music, playing a piece called “Okagura” on flutes and drums, and there is also the “mikomai”, danced to it with bells and fans.At the Sue district summer festival, Sue Elementary School’s wadaiko drum club performed.
comm_leg_fuku_p: A Soto Zen temple in the hills west of Okusa. It carries on the line of Hoshakuji, built in Noguchi by the lord of Okusa Castle in 1450. A ceramic hokyointo pagoda stands beside the gate, and a hall in the grounds enshrines the fire deity Akiba Sanjakubo. Every December, people walk over burning embers in the fire-walking rite, a prayer against fire.
comm_leg_g2: Festivals, performing arts, temples and shrines
comm_leg_hist_h: Oyama Temple Ruins and Chigo Shrine
comm_leg_hist_p: In Oyama are the ruins of Oyamamine Shofukuji, a temple thought to have been founded in the late 7th century: the “Oyama Temple Ruins”. It once flourished so much that people said “Enryakuji on Mt. Hiei in the west, Oyama Temple in the east”, but it was burned in an attack in the mid-12th century. It is a national historic site — one of only two in the city, with Komakiyama. Chigo Shrine to its south is said to have been built to console the spirits of two temple boys who died in the attack, and its approach, lined with nearly 100 cherry trees, is a well-known cherry-blossom spot. The city’s Komaki History Discovery Museum (こまき歴史発見館), on the 4th floor of Lapio with free admission, presents Komaki’s history through panels, videos and life-size graphics.
comm_leg_hotaru_p: The Oyama River crosses the east and is a large river where five streams, including the Ikeshita and Shinzo, meet. Upstream, the “Firefly Village” (Oyama-higashi) has been laid out as a rest area, and from early to mid-June Genji fireflies — now rarely seen — fly about. This scene too is one of the “Beautiful Aichi Landscape Resources”. Shinooka Elementary School raises fireflies from larvae and releases them into the Oyama River.
comm_leg_kama_h: Ancient kilns and the history of pottery
comm_leg_kama_p: From the 7th to the 11th century, the Shinooka district was, together with the Sanage kilns, a center of pottery making (ceramics) in the Owari region. More than 110 kiln sites have been found, known as the Shinooka Ancient Kiln Sites. They were half-underground “ana-gama” tunnel kilns, dug as narrow trenches into hill slopes and roofed with clay; Sue ware was fired in the 7th–8th centuries and ash-glazed ware from the late 9th century. Characters written on Sue ware from Shinooka Kiln No. 78 closely resemble those on Sue ware found at the Fujiwara capital in Nara, showing that Shinooka’s vessels travelled as far as Nara. “Shinooka Kiln Sites” is a name given to the remains in later times. The oldest example we could find in the National Diet Library search is the Komaki City Board of Education’s excavation report 『篠岡古窯址群』 (1971–72), so the name appears to date from the Showa era. We have not confirmed any record of the kilns being called this while they were in use. The city’s Komaki History Discovery Museum (こまき歴史発見館), on the 4th floor of Lapio with free admission, presents Komaki’s history through panels, videos and life-size graphics.
comm_leg_karuta_p: A local karuta card set on Shinooka Elementary School’s website. It turns the area’s history, ways of life and nature into 36 pairs of picture cards and explanation cards. Topics include how Shinooka Village came about, fireflies on the Oyama River, climbing kilns, the Battle of Komaki and Nagakute, bo-no-te, festival music and mikomai, peaches and grapes, Nagoya Cochin and bracken.
comm_leg_lead: Apart from the schools, the eastern district has traditions, festivals and local specialties that local people have handed down. They are the area’s heritage, and they go on even when the schools are reorganized.
comm_leg_mame_p: The endangered Mamenashi grows wild in Okusa. It is one of the “Tokai hill-zone plants” found only in the hills of the Tokai region, and the “Tara Mamenashi Village” has a walking path and signboards. Local groups hold viewing sessions in spring when it flowers and in autumn when it fruits.
comm_leg_matsuri_p: A summer event of Tokadai New Town, held every year in Tokadai Central Park, with bon-odori dancing, a flea market and food stalls. The 40th was held on 25–26 July 2026.
comm_leg_momo_p: The peach orchards on the eastern hills gave “Tokadai” (“peach-blossom heights”) its name, and the landscape (Kamisue) is one of Aichi Prefecture’s “Beautiful Aichi Landscape Resources”. “Shinooka peaches” are known nationwide for their large, very sweet fruit. They have been grown in Kamisue, Takane, Okusa and nearby for about 80 years, and at Toryo Junior High School students cook with eastern peaches grown by a parent.
comm_leg_more: This site’s view on how to carry on these traditions after the schools close (not the city’s view) is in In-depth review: “Carrying on the existing schools’ legacy”.
comm_leg_music_p: The citizens’ group Tokadai wo Kangaeru Kai has kept up the “Tokadai Music Festival” as a joint proposal project with the city’s Eastern District Development Office; November 2026 brings the 11th. The 7th, in November 2024 in the auditorium of the East Community Center, drew 240 people. At the 8th, in March 2025, a women’s choir and a residents’ band performed, and at the end the audience sang along. Tokadai Central Park also has an open-air stage, built in 2002.
comm_leg_name_list:
• 大草 (Okusa)14th century
  • 林 (Hayashi)Kamakura period
  • 野口 (Noguchi)Kamakura period
  • 陶 (Sue)Kamisue and Shimosue 1499; the name Sue 1889
  • 大山 (Oyama)Edo period
  • 池之内 (Ikenouchi)Edo period
  • 篠岡 (Shinooka)1906 (Shinooka Village)
comm_leg_name_more: The village history says the name refers to the two estates, but it does not say outright that one character was taken from each. Who chose the name is also unconfirmed. This site’s hypothesis about how it relates to the name “Tokadai” is in the page on the origin of the name.
comm_leg_name_p: As a place name, “Shinooka” can be confirmed from Shinooka Village in 1906. Earlier, in 1873, “Shinooka” can be confirmed as the name of a school. According to Seventy Years of Education in Shinooka (篠岡教育七十年), Shinooka School was founded in 1873 at a temple in Hayashi (Shounji, 祥雲寺), serving Hayashi, Noguchi and Oyama. According to the Shinooka Village History (1927), Okusa, Oyama and Noguchi belonged to the medieval Shinogi estate (篠木荘), and Hayashi, Ikenouchi, Kamisue and Shimosue to the Ajioka estate (味岡荘). In reference to this, the village was called Shinooka from the 1906 merger. The characters read as the “Shino” of Shinogi joined to the “oka” of Ajioka. The merger joined four villages: Okusa, Ono, Ikebayashi and Sue. What can be confirmed for 1873 is the name of a school; we do not know that the area was generally called “Shinooka” at that time.
comm_leg_okusa_p: A shrine in Okusa. At its festival on the second Sunday of each October, the Okusa Bo-no-te (Shinkage school), a city intangible folk cultural property, is offered. Its Thirty-Six Immortal Poets plaques (32 panels and a dedication plaque), thought to date from the late Edo period, became a city tangible folk cultural property in 2002 and are said to be the only such set from the Edo period in the city.
comm_leg_ondo_more: Read the lyrics and the hopes in them →
comm_leg_ondo_p: The “Shinooka Ondo”, also called the “Shin-Shinooka Ondo”, is a local song bearing the Shinooka name, loved as a bon-odori staple. A recording posted on a video-sharing site shows that it was released as a record.
comm_leg_peach_p: “Peachliner” was the nickname of the Tokadai Line, a new transit system that linked Tokadai New Town with Meitetsu Komaki Station. It opened on 25 March 1991 and ran 7.4 km on an elevated track from Komaki Station to Tokadai Higashi Station. All seven stations had platform screen doors, and only Komaki and Tokadai Center stations were staffed. Because the new town’s population grew less than expected, among other reasons, it kept losing money and was closed after its last day of service on 30 September 2006. Since that same September, the “Peach Bus” has run between Tokadai and Komaki Station in its place. Aichi Prefecture decided to remove the whole elevated line, and the removal has been carried out step by step. The former depot site in Hikarigaoka 6-chome became land owned jointly by the prefecture and the city, and part of it is used for parking and a pick-up and drop-off loop.
comm_leg_ryokudo_p: Tokadai New Town is a residential town that Aichi Prefecture built on about 322 ha of hills, and greenways (footpaths) run across it in every direction. This townscape has been chosen by the prefecture as a “Beautiful Aichi Landscape Resource”. Tokadai Parks No. 1 to No. 4 (about 2.0–2.7 ha each) are in Shiroyama, Momogaoka, Shinooka and Hikarigaoka, and Tokadai Nishi Park (about 4.15 ha) in Koga opened in 1980, the year residents began moving in. The parks and greenways have wisteria trellises and cherry trees. After the reorganization more children will walk to school along the greenways, and at briefings people have asked for more watching over them there.
comm_leg_shiki_p: A city park of about 28.2 hectares in Okusa. Besides the “Sorisuberi Hill” for sledding, the Wanpaku Adventure Plaza, the “Chibikko Animal Village” where children can touch animals, and the Rainbow Falls, it has a disc golf course, a park golf course and a barbecue area, and a monthly flower map shows what is in bloom. The view of its observation tower has been chosen by the prefecture as a “Beautiful Aichi Landscape Resource”. In summer 2024 a local group held a nature school here where parents and children observed insects and plants.
comm_leg_shoun_p: A Soto Zen temple in Hayashi, with the mountain name Shorinzan (少林山; written 小林山 in Edo-period gazetteers). It once belonged to Fukugonji in Okusa. It is said to have been written 正雲寺 until its name changed to the present characters in 1700, and records say it moved from low, damp ground to its present site in 1689. The Komaki City History dates its founding to the Bunsho era (1466–67), while the Edo-period Owari Junkoki (尾張徇行記) says the date is unknown. A community-founded school (義校) opened here in 1872 with 4 teachers and 79 children, and in 1873 Shinooka School was founded, serving Hayashi, Noguchi and Oyama. The school was renamed Hayashi School in 1876. Today the temple stays connected with the community through Zen meditation, sutra copying and markets.
comm_leg_sky_p: A 33-story, 110.6-meter apartment building with 270 homes in Shinooka 1-chome, completed in 1991. Visible from all over the town, it is one of the landmarks of the Tokadai skyline. People live there, so it is not a place to visit.
comm_leg_src: Sources are shown under each card. PDF materials are listed by title only. The wisteria trellises and cherry trees, autumn festivals around the east, and the origin of the Shin-Shinooka Ondo, could not be confirmed from published materials. For the latest dates, please check with each group or organizer.
comm_leg_stadium_p: The baseball ground of the city’s sports complex in Kamisue, also called the “Shimin Kyūjō” (citizens’ ballpark). It was completed in 1988. The foul lines are 92 meters and center field 120 meters, with long-pile artificial turf, floodlights and an indoor practice area. The multipurpose ground next to it is used for softball, football (soccer) and athletics. In the east, the Komaki Sports Association’s junior soccer also plays at places such as Sue Ground and the Hikarigaoka Junior High field (community clubs).
comm_leg_tkpark_p: A park of about 6.4 ha in Shiroyama 2-chome, opened in April 1992. It has a wide lawn and a fountain, a long roller slide, an adventure playground and a suspension bridge, and a walking trail through nature on its 100-meter hill. An open-air stage was added in 2002, and the summer Tokadai Festival is held here. The city says it plans to hold exchange events between elementary schools in this park, so that children get used to their new surroundings before the reorganization.
comm_leg_tower_h: The water tower on the hill
comm_leg_tower_p: The Tokadai Elevated Water Tank stands on the hill in Tokadai Central Park. Built by Aichi Prefecture in 1981 to supply higher-lying areas, it went into service in 1991 and passed to Komaki City in 1995. It is 29.4 m tall, its tank holds about 600 m³, and it supplies about 3,500 m³ a day. Its brown color comes from weathering steel, whose rust layer protects the metal beneath.
comm_leg_winery_p: A winery in Noguchi, opened in April 2015 by the social welfare corporation AJU Jiritsu no Ie. People with disabilities do the work, from growing the grapes to making and selling the wine. A “Spring Wine Festival” was held there in May 2024. A project that turned the grape pomace left over from winemaking into bread and recipes, together with a local bakery, a university and the city, was also carried out as an Eastern District trial activity.
comm_list_intro: All five elementary school districts in the Shinooka area have a Community Council, and all five were certified by the city on April 1, 2020. The oldest, Sue Elementary District, was founded in 2014 and has over a decade of activity behind it.
comm_list_note:
Note: Each council publishes an annual activity plan and budget on the city website (the FY2026 documents are currently posted). Source: Komaki City, "Establishment and activities of Community Councils" (updated June 4, 2026). Representatives' names are personal information and are not reproduced here.
For the latest information and details on each council, see the city's Community Council page.
comm_pf_h: Eastern District Town Development Platform<small>東部まちづくりプラットフォーム</small>
comm_pf_link_about: About the Eastern District Town Development Platform (Komaki City, Japanese)
comm_pf_link_form: Registration form (logo form linked by the city, Japanese)
comm_pf_p1: A space the city opened, based on the Eastern District Development Concept it adopted in March 2022, for people involved in the east’s town development to connect. Residents, businesses, schools and other educational institutions, and the city register, share information and find partners to act with. The city likens it to a station platform: not a destination, but a place where people meet on their way to the next step.
comm_pf_p2: Anyone interested can register, not only people who live in the eastern district. After agreeing to the terms and registering, you receive from the city’s Eastern District Development Office an invitation to an online space on LINE OpenChat, and notices of in-person gatherings such as discussion meetings, workshops and town-development seminars.
comm_pf_src: Source: Komaki City, “東部まちづくりプラットフォームとは？”. Rewritten by this site after reading the city’s page; not the city’s own wording.
comm_qa1_a: The city has announced a policy of reorganizing to 2 Community Councils by FY2029, but how the integration proceeds and how each event will be handled will be determined through consultations with residents and the individual councils. At this point, many details about how activities will be handed over remain undecided, and it is hoped that a forum will be provided for residents' voices to be reflected.
comm_qa1_q: What will happen to current activities when the councils are reduced to two?
comm_qa2_a: Schools have served as hubs for community events, disaster preparedness, sports, and childcare. School consolidation means the number of these hubs will change, but the city has declared a policy of continuing community use of closed school facilities, so gymnasiums and sports fields are expected to remain available. How to rebuild the community itself will need to be discussed with residents taking the lead.
comm_qa2_q: Won't community bonds weaken if the local school disappears?
comm_qa3_a: They won't disappear. New School Management Councils (Community Schools) will be organized in each of the 4 new schools after reorganization (Tokadai Higashi Elementary, Tokadai Nishi Elementary, Tokadai Higashi Junior High, Tokadai Nishi Junior High). However, how to carry on the relationships and activities cultivated by each current school's Community School depends on future consultations. A joint school management council of the eight schools is planned for December 2026 (“Shinooka School Reorganization News” No. 4).
comm_qa3_q: Will Community School activities disappear with the school consolidation?
comm_qa4_a: Events that each Community Council has organized over many years (disaster drills, children's events, local festivals, etc.) are activities carried out by local residents. Even after the councils are integrated, continuation is possible based on the will and consensus of local residents, but the specific form will be at the discretion of the new post-reorganization councils. No official policy has yet been announced.
comm_qa4_q: What will happen to local events that each community has independently continued?
comm_row1_after: To be reorganized into 2 councils; transition to new structure planned for FY2029. Specific groupings are currently under review.
comm_row1_now: 5 councils in Shinooka area (one per elementary school district)
comm_row2_after: Will be newly organized in each of the 4 new schools after reorganization. (From official Komaki City Q&A, Q11)
comm_row2_now: Established at each school (currently covering 8 schools)
comm_row3_after: Even after consolidation, gymnasiums and sports grounds of closed schools will in principle be retained as "important community bases for local sports and disaster preparedness."
comm_row3_now: Community use of each school's facilities
comm_row4_after: Placement by school district will continue. After the reorganization, clubs are to be set up inside Tokadai Higashi and Tokadai Nishi elementary schools.
comm_row5_after: Consolidation will expand the activity area. Continuity of existing events and activities will be decided through discussions within each council and community.
comm_row5_now: Each council hosts its own community-specific events
